newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian stocks rally again, but caution creeps in.
newsitem.headline: Italian stocks rally again, but caution creeps in.

text.p: Italy's stock market bounded higher on Monday in the third day of big rises as investors continued to be attracted by equity yields, but many analysts turned cautious after a number of false dawns on the Milan market.

With the Milan stock market up nearly ten percent over the last three days, many saw this rally unable to be maintained at such levels unless signs continue of domestic funds switching into equities from Italian investors' favoured government bonds.

As the Italian domestic bond market has roared away over the last few months with prices setting new all-time highs, bond yields for investors have slipped helping to put a brighter outlook on the often-neglected Italian equity market.

First signs of a switch into equities from bonds came last Wednesday when fund management association, Assogestioni, reported net subscriptions to mutual funds had overtaken redemptions for the first time in two years during December, and indications for January suggest this inflow is continuing.
"In the medium term, the rally can continue if these indications are maintained for January and February," said equity stategist Marco Nascimbeni at brokers Carnegie in Milan.

Another investment house predicted that if only five percent of domestic funds in Italian bonds switched into equities this would account for some four trillion lire ($2.6 billion) of new money, which would help equities but was unlikely to propel the stock market to new record levels.

Despite the New Year share rally, the major indicators of the Italian market were still off record highs although the March futures FIB contract for Italy's top stocks in the Mib 30 index hit a new high of 17,890 since its start in late 1994.
"Futures show the potential short-term direction, but we are still a long way off record highs in the major market indices," said another Milan equity strategist.

The Mib30 index closed up 2.24 percent at 17,520, but was below its record high of over 18,000 hit in early 1994. The value of this index of Italy's largest 30 quoted companies was set at 10,000 at end-1992.

The most historic index stretching back to 1972, the Comit, calculated at the end of each trading day, closed at 710.26 on January 10 from the 100 set in 1972, but the index was way off its record high of 908 reached on May 20 1986.

Strategists pointed out that in a liquidity-starved stock market such as Milan, small influxes of fund money can produce disproportion reactions, helped by the relative poor performance of the bourse in 1996 which made Milan stocks relatively cheap.

Domestic investors have long favoured the steady returns of the bond market, but yields of these investments have fallen to around five percent net, compared to double digit yields some months ago. They now have to weigh up a move to the greater returns but also greater risks of equities.
Strategists were wary of the sharp rise as foreign investors had been generally quiet as prices have risen, while the rally has been across the board and not particularly stock selective.

"These are early days to assess the move, given the small size of the equity market. What the different is this time is the low yield for alternative investments, but will the cautious Italian investor be attacted out of bonds," said one strategist.

The stock rally has also been supported by the continued strength in domestic bonds and the lira, and overseas stock markets. On Friday, Wall Street hit its fourth high of the year, while German and French shares reached record highs on Monday. ($1=1,546 lire)
